mechanisms.name: Texas Backup Power Package Program (16 TAC 25.513, PUCT Project No. 59024)
mechanisms.what_it_is: Texas Energy Fund grants and forgivable loans pay an approved vendor to install a behind-the-meter backup package at a critical facility (hospital, police/fire station, water plant, shelter, school, house of worship). The critical-facility owner signs an award agreement with the commission and a contract with a commission-selected vendor; the facility owner controls the site and owns the package. Grant is capped at $500 per kilowatt; anything above that must be financed by the forgivable loan. Costs funded by the award may not be recovered from the facility's customers or constituents.
mechanisms.who_signs: Critical-facility owner <-> PUCT / Texas Energy Fund administrator (award agreement), plus facility owner <-> commission-approved vendor (install + service)
mechanisms.term: Compliance and monitoring period set in the award agreement; site control (ownership or lease) required for its duration
mechanisms.price_form: grant-funded, capped at $500/kW, plus forgivable loan for the balance

precedents.name: Hydrogen / fuel-cell eligibility request denied
precedents.parties: FCHEA, GTL Leasing, Sharper Energy Technologies, Texas Hydrogen Alliance, Schneider Electric vs. PUCT
precedents.size: requested addition of hydrogen, ammonia, alkanes and fuel cells to 25.513(b)(3)(A)(vi)
precedents.note: Denied on statutory grounds — the clearest available evidence that the eligible-generation list is closed and enumerated, not performance-based.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Excluded by construction, and the exclusion has now been tested. Adopted 25.513(b)(3)(A)(vi) requires a package to 'provide power sourced from a combination of natural gas or propane with photovoltaic panels and battery storage,' and new subparagraph (vii) requires it to 'prioritize power sourced from natural gas when it is available on site.' When five parties asked to add hydrogen and fuel cells, the commission refused 'because the statute does not authorize inclusion of alternative fuel sources' — so the list is a closed statutory enumeration a nuclear unit cannot enter by demonstrating equivalent performance. The 48-continuous-hour-without-refuelling rule is the one criterion a reactor passes trivially and a diesel set fails without a fuel farm, but it buys nothing here because eligibility gates on fuel type first. The no-export rule (b)(3)(A)(iii) and (b)(3)(B) additionally forbid the wholesale or retail sale of energy, ancillary services, ERS, ADER participation, solar buyback, or any demand-response participation — so a host cannot monetise off-hours output, which is the entire economic case for putting a baseload reactor behind a 2.5 MW critical load.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: The 2.5 MW cap and the definition of 'critical load' (life-safety, medical, emergency comms, potable water) size these packages exactly in the 1-20 MW microreactor band's bottom end — but the cap is on critical load, not on the resource, and the no-export prohibition means the other 90% of a microreactor's annual output would be curtailed. A Texas critical facility is a good technical fit and a terrible TBPP fit; the honest path is the loan side of the Texas Energy Fund or a separate ESA, not this rule.
blockers: 16 TAC 25.513(b)(3)(A)(vi) enumerates natural gas or propane + PV + battery storage — a closed list, not a performance standard
25.513(b)(3)(A)(vii): must prioritize natural gas when available on site
25.513(b)(3)(A)(iii) and (b)(3)(B): controls must prevent any sale of energy, ancillary services, ERS or other reliability service; no ADER, no solar buyback, no demand response
Commission declined hydrogen/fuel cells 'because the statute does not authorize inclusion of alternative fuel sources' — changing the list requires the Legislature, not the PUCT
Vendors must be selected by the commission through a competitive solicitation and kept on an approved vendor list
$500/kW grant cap is roughly two orders of magnitude below microreactor capex

mechanisms.name: Utility-owned community microgrid via CPCN + rate base (ICC Docket 17-0331, ComEd Bronzeville)
mechanisms.what_it_is: ComEd petitioned the Illinois Commerce Commission for a certificate of public convenience and necessity to build, own and rate-base a full-feeder community microgrid serving roughly 1,060 customers and about 7 MW of peak load across 0.29 square miles of Bronzeville, Chicago. The utility owns the wires, the microgrid master controller and the storage; non-storage DER was to be competitively procured from third parties which the utility would not own. The whole capital cost goes into ComEd's distribution rate base and is recovered from all 3.9 million ComEd customers, not from the 1,060 inside the boundary.
mechanisms.who_signs: ComEd <-> Illinois Commerce Commission (CPCN petition), with a side agreement ComEd <-> Citizens Utility Board / Environmental Defense Fund on a future pilot microgrid services tariff
mechanisms.term: Multi-year study period with Annual Reports to the docket (the eighth annual report was filed 2026-02-27)

precedents.name: ICC Docket 17-0331 — ComEd Bronzeville Community Microgrid, Final Order
precedents.parties: Commonwealth Edison Co.; ICC Staff; Illinois Attorney General; Citizens Utility Board; Environmental Defense Fund; Environmental Law & Policy Center; Illinois Power Agency
precedents.size: approx. 7 MW peak load, 1,060 customers, 0.29 sq mi; Phase I 2.5 MW load + 0.75 MW PV + 0.5 MW / 2 MWh BESS + up to 3 MW of ComEd's existing mobile diesel gensets; Phase II adds 4.5 MW load and ~7 MW of controllable generation
precedents.price: $29.6M gross; $25M maximum net to ComEd after a $4M DOE SHINES grant and $600,000 partner cost-share; ~$200,000/yr operating cost
precedents.note: Order entered 2018-02-28. Staff's smaller alternative would have cost about $12.3M less. Phase I net cost approx. $8M.

precedents.name: ComEd / CUB / EDF agreement to file a pilot microgrid services tariff
precedents.parties: ComEd <-> Citizens Utility Board and Environmental Defense Fund
precedents.size: third-party-developed microgrids using ComEd wires; utility feasibility study on customer request; islanding services and the utility microgrid controller offered under tariff
precedents.note: Committed filing date no later than 2020-01-01 — but the Commission itself declined to endorse it, holding tariff findings premature.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: This is the cleanest US template for putting a generator inside a utility's rate base rather than selling its output: the host community signs nothing, pays nothing directly, and the cost is socialised across the whole service territory. That structure would carry a microreactor's capex without a creditworthy offtaker — but 17-0331 also shows the price of admission. The Attorney General's central attack was cost-per-benefit on a $25M asset serving 1,060 customers, and the order's own framing is that '$25 million ... sets the bar for the' benefits the project must show. A reactor at 5-10x that capex faces the same prudence test with a far bigger number, plus a siting question the order never had to reach. Note also that ComEd's existing tariffs 'prohibit the use of customer-owned generation as a source of' supply inside the microgrid — utility ownership was not merely preferred, it was the path of least tariff resistance.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: The Bronzeville footprint is 7 MW of peak load — the exact middle of the 1-20 MW microreactor band, and one unit would replace both the 3 MW of mobile diesel gensets ComEd planned to wheel in for testing and the 7 MW of Phase II controllable generation. A single relocatable unit also collapses the two-phase build (Phase I to satisfy a DOE grant deadline, Phase II for the real microgrid) into one asset.
blockers: CPCN prudence test: the AG argued a reasonable person would not invest $25 million on the demonstrated benefits; the reliability benefit was computed from LBNL/DOE ICE Calculator values
Public Utilities Act Section 9-241 non-discrimination — spending rate-base dollars concentrated in one neighbourhood was litigated as an unlawful preference
The Commission expressly refused to bless the third-party microgrid tariff: 'any findings on tariffs are premature in this docket'
ComEd's existing tariffs prohibit customer-owned generation as a supply source inside its system, pushing ownership to the utility
Cost allocation across customer classes was deferred to a future tariff filing, leaving recovery unresolved at order date

mechanisms.name: California Self-Generation Incentive Program — 2025 Handbook eligibility gates (CPUC SGIP)
mechanisms.what_it_is: SGIP pays a capacity-based rebate to a Host Customer (or their assigned Payee) for behind-the-meter storage and generation installed on the customer side of the utility meter. The Host Customer owns or leases the equipment, or takes it under a lease/PPA/energy-services agreement — the handbook expressly allows PPAs — and the Program Administrator (PG&E, SCE, SoCalGas, or the Center for Sustainable Energy) pays the incentive against milestone documentation, with performance-based payments metered by an approved Performance Data Provider for five years. The host bears all performance risk; the incentive is a one-time capex offset, not an energy price. Three earlier-pass claims are now confirmed from the handbook itself: the eligible-equipment list is a closed enumeration, there is a 40% minimum electric-efficiency gate expressed as E/F_HHV, and equipment intended solely for emergency backup is ineligible.
mechanisms.who_signs: Host Customer <-> SGIP Program Administrator (PG&E / SCE / SoCalGas / Center for Sustainable Energy), under the SGIP Contract; separate host <-> installer/owner agreements (lease, PPA or energy-services agreement) must be handed to the PA
mechanisms.term: 10-year warranty / contractual-permanence period; 5 years of Performance Data Provider metering; 10-year renewable-fuel audit for fuelled projects
mechanisms.price_form: one-time $/W or $/Wh capacity rebate (grant-funded from ratepayer collections)

precedents.price: $813,400,000 total authorized collections; reservations issued through 2025-12-31

precedents.name: Generation incentive rates and the 3 MW ceiling (2025 Handbook Tables 4.1.3 and 4.2.3)
precedents.parties: CPUC Energy Division / SGIP Program Administrators
precedents.size: incentives paid for up to 3 MW of rated capacity; 100% of base to 1 MW, 75% for >1-2 MW, 50% for >2-3 MW, 0% above 3 MW

precedents.note: A 3 MW unit taking base + resiliency adder tops out around $9.4M of incentive; a 10 MW unit gets the same $9.4M, because everything above 3 MW earns 0%.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Excluded three separate ways, any one of which is fatal. (1) The eligible-equipment list is a closed enumeration — storage plus eleven named generation technologies (pressure reduction turbines, PV, wind, gas turbines, waste heat to power, microturbines, steam turbine CHP, internal combustion engines, linear generators, fuel cell CHP, fuel cell electric) — with no performance-based route in. (2) The generation budget is a *renewable* generation budget: 'Eligible fuels are those that produce useful energy when undergoing combustion or a chemical reaction and are classified as renewable', and customers 'are required to use 100% renewable fuel for the lifetime of the project'. Fission is neither combustion nor a chemical reaction, and is not renewable in California law. (3) The 40% electrical-efficiency gate is written as E/F_HHV, a ratio of rated electric output to *higher heating value fuel consumption* — a quantity that is undefined for a reactor, so the qualifying test cannot even be evaluated, let alone passed. Separately, the ineligibility of 'Backup systems intended solely for emergency purposes' is confirmed verbatim, and it cuts against diesel gensets as well: an emergency-only genset cannot claim SGIP either.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: SGIP is the clearest place a *relocatable* microreactor is worse off than a fixed one. The handbook's permanence test says only systems permanently installed 'both physically and contractually' are eligible, and it names the disqualifiers: 'unsecured equipment, wheels, carrying handles, dolly, trailer, or platform, will deem the system ineligible'. Factory-built, truck-delivered, take-it-back-at-end-of-life is the microreactor's whole product story and it is the exact fact pattern this clause rejects. The 60-day written notice required before any change of site location or system ownership within the warranty period compounds it. The 3 MW incentive ceiling also caps the subsidy at the very bottom of the 1-20 MW band.
blockers: Eligible Equipment is a closed enumerated list of storage plus 11 named generation technologies; no equivalent-performance pathway
Renewable Fuel Eligibility (Sec. 7.4): eligible fuels must undergo combustion or a chemical reaction AND be classified as renewable; 100% renewable fuel required for project life
Operational eligibility (Sec. 7.1): waste-heat utilisation >=5% per P.U. Code 216.6(a), or Electrical Efficiency E/F_HHV >= 40% — both defined over fuel heating value
Ineligible Equipment: 'Backup systems intended solely for emergency purposes'; also any generation capable of operating on or switching to diesel fuel for start-up or continuous operation
Permanent-installation test rejects any indication of portability (wheels, trailer, platform, quick disconnects)
Incentive rated-capacity ceiling of 3 MW, declining from 100% to 0% between 1 MW and 3 MW
Ineligible customer class: any electrical corporation under P.U. Code 218 that generates or purchases electricity for wholesale or retail sale
Rebuilt, refurbished or relocated equipment is ineligible

mechanisms.name: AEP Ohio Schedule DCT (Data Center Tariff), P.U.C.O. No. 22 Sheet 223 — large-load minimum-demand tariff
mechanisms.what_it_is: A data centre with an aggregate monthly maximum demand above 25,000 kW at a single location (or aggregated across affiliates in the service territory) signs an Electric Service Agreement with Ohio Power Company under Schedule DCT, plus a Letter of Agreement and a Contribution in Aid of Construction agreement for customer-specific plant. The customer commits to a Contract Capacity for an initial term of the Load Ramp Period plus 8 years and pays a minimum monthly billing demand whether or not it consumes the power, so the utility — not the customer — is protected against stranded network investment. Collateral of 50% of total minimum charges over the whole term is posted at signing unless the customer is A-/A3 rated with liquidity above 10x that amount. The customer must own or hold the exclusive right to use a designated site before signing.
mechanisms.who_signs: Data-centre customer <-> Ohio Power Company (AEP Ohio), under an ESA + Letter of Agreement + CIAC agreement, on tariff terms approved by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio
mechanisms.term: Load Ramp Period (max 4 years) plus 8 years — so 12 years only when the ramp runs the full 4; 3-year ramp gives 11. Thereafter evergreen on 3 years' written notice.
mechanisms.price_form: rate-based: $8.08/kW primary or $9.05/kW secondary distribution demand charge, plus customer charge and all approved riders, applied to a contractual minimum billing demand

precedents.parties: AEP Ohio (Ohio Power Company); PUCO Staff; Office of the Ohio Consumers' Counsel; and other signatory parties
precedents.size: applies to new data-centre load above 25,000 kW aggregate, and to existing customers expanding by more than 25,000 kW
precedents.price: minimum billing demand floor; exit fee of 36 months of minimum charges, available only after the fifth year following the ramp

precedents.name: Minimum Demand table and Load Ramp floors, Schedule DCT Sheets 223-1 and 223-4
precedents.parties: Ohio Power Company, issued by Marc Reitter, President, AEP Ohio
precedents.size: Load Ramp Contract Capacity floors of 50% / 65% / 80% / 90% of Contract Capacity in years 1-4
precedents.price: 25,001-75,000 kW: 15,000 kW plus 85% of the marginal amount over 25,000 kW. 75,001 kW and above: 57,500 kW plus 100% of the marginal amount over 75,000 kW, capped at 85% of total contract capacity. Existing Load floor is 60%.
precedents.note: CORRECTION to the widely reported '85% minimum demand': 85% is the marginal rate in the lower band and the overall cap in the upper band, not the floor. A 25 MW new load's floor is 15 MW = 60% of contract capacity; the marginal rate above 75 MW is 100%, not 85%.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Ignores nuclear — and that neutrality is the opening. Schedule DCT never enumerates generation technologies. Its 'Customer-Owned Generation and Emergency Conditions' section lets a customer elect to use behind-the-meter generation to offset its Contract Capacity, on one engineering condition: equipment must exist 'to instantaneously curtail load equal to or greater than the behind-the-meter generation output', plus an OAC 4901:1-22 interconnection agreement. Because the customer's exposure is a minimum billing demand rather than metered consumption, a BTM generator that merely shaves energy saves nothing — only lowering Contract Capacity itself does. That makes the netting election the single most valuable clause in the tariff for a reactor developer: every MW of firm on-site capacity that reduces Contract Capacity removes roughly 0.85 MW of minimum billing demand for the full 11-12 year term, and reduces the 50%-of-minimum-charges collateral in proportion. Emergency or backup generation not designed to run in parallel is expressly outside these requirements — the escape hatch a diesel farm uses and a baseload reactor cannot.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: A 25 MW data centre is the smallest load Schedule DCT reaches, and it is served entirely by the top of the 1-20 MW microreactor band or a two-unit plant — so the microreactor is the only reactor class that can address the tariff's entry tier rather than only hyperscale campuses. The instantaneous-curtailment requirement is also easier to satisfy for a small, steadily-loaded unit than for a large one whose trip drops a step the site cannot absorb. Against that, the tariff's site rule ('must own or have the exclusive right to use the land') and the 8-year-post-ramp commitment are indifferent to relocatability, so the microreactor's mobility earns nothing here.
blockers: Minimum billing demand is owed 'regardless of the customer choosing to curtail, reduce, suspend, or terminate service' during the initial term
Exit only after the fifth year following the Load Ramp Period, and only on paying 36 months of minimum charges
Collateral of 50% of total minimum charges for the full term unless rated A- (S&P) and A3 (Moody's) with liquidity above 10x that requirement
Netting BTM output against Contract Capacity requires instantaneous load-curtailment equipment maintained for the term, subject to the transmission provider's technical requirements
Service may be suspended with Commission approval if usage exceeds Contract Capacity by more than 1,000 kW — including for customers with BTM generation
New Loads are barred from the 1CP and 6CP Basic Transmission Cost Rider programs
Affiliate aggregation: all affiliated New Load above 25,000 kW is stacked by energization date to compute Minimum Demand
Service does not commence 'until the Company has sufficient capacity to meet the contractual load requirements' — the queue, not the contract, sets the date

mechanisms.name: Indiana Michigan Power Tariff I.P. large-load terms (IURC Cause No. 46097) — the second-state comparison to AEP Ohio
mechanisms.what_it_is: Indiana Michigan Power's Industrial Power tariff was modified by an unopposed settlement among I&M, the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor, Citizens Action Coalition, Amazon Data Services, the Data Center Coalition, Google and Microsoft, approved by the IURC on 2025-02-19. A customer at or above 70 MW at one plant, or 150 MW aggregated across affiliated premises of 1 MW or more, becomes a 'Large Load Customer' and signs an Electric Services Agreement fixing contract capacity, load ramp and term. Minimum monthly billing demand never falls below 80% of contract capacity, and collateral equals 24 times the maximum monthly non-fuel bill. Same commercial idea as AEP Ohio Schedule DCT, materially different numbers — which is why running both matters.
mechanisms.who_signs: Large Load Customer <-> Indiana Michigan Power Company, via an Electric Services Agreement under Tariff I.P., approved by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission
mechanisms.term: Initial Contract Term not less than 12 years, which begins only AFTER a Load Ramp Period of up to 5 years — a total commitment of up to 17 years. 42 months' written notice to discontinue.
mechanisms.price_form: rate-based; minimum monthly charge = monthly service charge + minimum demand charge x monthly billing demand + Step 1 embedded capacity charge x billing demand + energy blocks

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Ignores nuclear, and then closes the door the Ohio tariff leaves open. Tariff I.P.'s Special Terms are explicit that a customer with its own generation buys standby service and must 'contract for the maximum amount of demand in kW which the Company might be required to furnish' — so behind-the-meter generation does not reduce the contracted demand, it defines it. Layered on the 80% minimum billing demand, a Large Load Customer with an on-site reactor still owes 80% of a contract capacity sized to full backup. Worse, the tariff's standing path for customer generation routes to 'Rider NMS (Net Metering Service Rider), Tariff COGEN/SPP or by special agreement with the Company' — and a fission plant is neither a cogeneration facility nor a PURPA small power production facility, whose fuel must be biomass, waste, renewable resources or geothermal. A reactor host in I&M territory therefore has exactly one route, the bilateral special agreement, with no tariffed terms to fall back on. This is the sharpest contrast in the file: Ohio lets BTM output offset Contract Capacity subject to instantaneous curtailment; Indiana makes BTM output irrelevant to the bill.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: Nothing helpful, and that is the finding. The 70 MW single-plant threshold is 2.8x AEP Ohio's 25 MW, so no single microreactor and no plausible small fleet reaches the tier at all — a 1-20 MW unit is invisible to this tariff except as the on-site generator of a customer who is already there for other reasons. The 150 MW affiliate-aggregation rule with a 1 MW per-premises floor also means a distributed fleet of small sites can be swept into Large Load status collectively while no individual site qualifies for anything.
blockers: 80% minimum monthly billing demand floor on contract capacity, and on the highest billing demand of the past 11 months
Standby/backup service requires contracting for the full maximum demand the Company might have to furnish — BTM generation cannot reduce it
Customer generation routed to Rider NMS, Tariff COGEN/SPP, or a bilateral special agreement; nuclear qualifies for neither PURPA category
Initial Contract Term of 12 years starts only after a Load Ramp Period of up to 5 years
42 months' written notice, aligned to the PJM Delivery Year, before any reduction or termination
Any mutually agreed reduction beyond 20% must be approved by the Commission (Ordering Paragraph 3)
Collateral of 24x the maximum monthly non-fuel bill, recomputed annually, unless A-/A3 rated with 10x liquidity
Large Load Customer reports are confidential trade secret under Ind. Code 24-2-3-2 — the comparables are sealed

mechanisms.name: New Jersey Town Center DER Microgrid Program, Phases I and II (NJBPU Docket No. QO16100967)
mechanisms.what_it_is: A post-Sandy state programme in which a municipality, county or state agency that owns critical facilities applies to the NJ Board of Public Utilities for a cash incentive, first to fund a feasibility study (Phase I) and then, competitively, to fund the engineering design of a 'Town Center DER Microgrid' — a cluster of FEMA Category III and IV critical facilities inside one municipal boundary, connected to DER that can island from the grid. The awardee signs an MOU with the Board, takes 75% of the award on execution and 25% on Staff's verification that the delivered design matches the application. The public agency owns the asset and bears every downstream risk; the Board funds paper, not steel, and states explicitly that an award 'does not indicate Board approval of any TCDER Microgrid project'.
mechanisms.who_signs: Municipality / county / state agency <-> New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, via a Memorandum of Understanding executed within 60 days of the order
mechanisms.term: Design-stage only; MOU plus quarterly status reports to Board Staff and six-monthly meetings with the electric distribution company
mechanisms.price_form: grant-funded design incentive (75% on MOU execution, 25% on Staff design review)

precedents.name: Phase I TCDER Microgrid Feasibility Study Incentive Program
precedents.parties: NJBPU and 13 applicants: Atlantic City, Camden County, Cape May County MUA, Galloway, Highland Park, Hoboken, Hudson County, Middletown, Montclair, Neptune, Paterson, NJ Treasury (Trenton), Woodbridge

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Ignores nuclear — the eligibility rule is about which BUILDINGS are in the cluster, not which machine powers it — and it contains the single most useful regulator finding in this file for a firm non-emitting resource. The Board found that 'existing technology and cost considerations currently do not allow for renewable DERs alone, or renewable DERs coupled with energy storage, to provide the level and length of resilience that critical facilities need' and therefore that 'the inclusion of fossil fueled DER in TCDER Phase II Incentive Program projects is necessary at this time'. Every one of the eight funded designs proves it: each carries natural gas CHP or gas/diesel gensets, and the Board simultaneously URGES awardees to minimise fossil DER. That is a regulator publicly stating a capability gap it cannot close with the technologies on its own list. The gating constraint for a reactor is not eligibility but the applicant's own certification that the project 'is legally permissible' under existing law, code and standing Board Orders — which for a multi-building municipal cluster means crossing public streets, and therefore squarely raises New Jersey's right-of-way question.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: The size match is almost exact and it is measured, not asserted: six of the eight funded designs sit between 1.7 MW and 4.4 MW, and the median awarded project is about 2.5 MW. A single 1-20 MW unit covers any of them, and covers the two 20 MW outliers (Atlantic City, Trenton) as a small fleet. Crucially these are multi-day-outage resilience assets whose fossil DER exists precisely because storage cannot hold the duration — the one attribute a reactor has for free. The programme's own money is far too small (a $196K-$1.1M design grant) to matter, so the value here is the documented demand shape and the named counterparties, not the funding.
blockers: Board FINDS fossil-fuelled DER 'necessary at this time' — the incumbent is written into the record, not merely tolerated

mechanisms.name: Connecticut Microgrid Grant and Loan Program (Public Act 12-148 Sec. 7) — the per-site civic-resilience cost dataset
mechanisms.what_it_is: Connecticut's post-Irene/Sandy statute directed DEEP to run a microgrid grant and loan programme for critical facilities. A municipality, electric distribution company, municipal electric utility, energy improvement district or private entity applies in a competitive round; DEEP awards a grant or loan and the recipient owns and operates the microgrid, reporting annually to PURA, the Office of Consumer Counsel, DEEP and two legislative committees for five years. The decisive statutory limit is on what the money buys: under the pilot the grants and loans pay only for design, engineering services and interconnection infrastructure — not the generator. A 2016 bond expansion widened this to matching funds or low-interest loans for energy storage and clean distributed generation. DEEP's own award-tracking chart is the per-site dataset: 12 operational microgrids and $22,265,935 of awards.
mechanisms.who_signs: Municipality, EDC, municipal electric utility, energy improvement district or private entity <-> Connecticut Department of Energy & Environmental Protection, following a competitive Request for Proposals/Applications
mechanisms.term: Grant or loan; recipient must report project status annually for five years to PURA, OCC, DEEP and the appropriations and energy committees
mechanisms.price_form: grant-funded (and low-interest loans), restricted by statute to design, engineering services and interconnection infrastructure

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Admits a reactor by construction — the only mechanism in this file that does. Public Act 12-148 Sec. 7(a)(3) defines the eligible resource purely by size and location: 'the generation of electricity from a unit with a rating of not more than sixty-five megawatts on the premises of a retail end user'. There is no fuel list, no emissions test, no efficiency gate and no renewability requirement — the exact opposite of the PUCT's closed natural-gas-or-propane enumeration and the CPUC's combustion-or-chemical-reaction-and-renewable fuel rule. A 1-20 MW reactor on a hospital or municipal campus satisfies the definition on its face. The statutory 'critical facility' list is equally accommodating: hospital, police station, fire station, water treatment plant, sewage treatment plant, public shelter, correctional facility, any commercial area of a municipality, a municipal centre, or anything else DEEP identifies as critical. The catch is on the money, not the eligibility: the pilot grant may fund only design, engineering services and interconnection infrastructure, so a reactor developer gets its wires and controls paid for and none of its capex.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: Two things. First, the 65 MW statutory ceiling is written as a maximum, so a smaller unit is strictly safer under it while a full-size reactor is excluded outright — this is one of the few rules where being small is legally load-bearing rather than merely commercially convenient. Second, the delivered fleet shows what a reactor would be replacing: ten of the twelve operational Connecticut microgrids are anchored on natural gas CHP, fuel cells or diesel, and the only battery-led project kept a natural gas generator on site anyway. On capacity the fit is direct — the built systems run from about 200 kW to 4.2 MW, so a single unit at the bottom of the microreactor band covers any of them and most of them several times over.
blockers: PA 12-148 Sec. 7(c): grants and loans may only fund design, engineering services and interconnection infrastructure — no generation capex under the pilot authority
Statutory pilot cap of $15,000,000 total (PA 13-298 later authorised a further $30,000,000)
No open Request for Applications; DEEP's programme page states none is currently open and its content was last updated January 2020
Award-to-operation attrition is high: 7 of 9 pilot awards and 1 of 3 Round 4 awards appear as operational in DEEP's tracker
Five years of annual status reporting to PURA, OCC, DEEP and two legislative committees
Awards were to be distributed as evenly as possible between small, medium and large municipalities — a political allocation rule, not a technical one

mechanisms.name: New Jersey 'on-site generation facility' carve-out from public-utility status (NJBPU Docket No. QO20030191, DCO Energy declaratory ruling)
mechanisms.what_it_is: New Jersey's Electric Discount and Energy Competition Act creates a narrow exemption from the incumbent utility's exclusive franchise: a generator that sells electricity to a single end-use customer located on the same or contiguous property is an 'on-site generation facility' and, by statute, is not a public utility. The developer owns and operates the plant, signs one power purchase agreement with one host, and the host is exempt from the Societal Benefits Charge, Market Transition Charge and Transition Bond Charge on that power. DCO Energy petitioned the Board on 2020-02-28 to confirm that adding the AtlantiCare Regional Medical Center to its 6 MW CHP at the Midtown Thermal Control Center qualified, even though the hospital sits diagonally across an intersection 145 feet door-to-door. Atlantic City Electric intervened and opposed. The Board granted the petition on 2021-01-27.
mechanisms.who_signs: Developer <-> host, under a single power purchase agreement for the whole campus (DCO Energy <-> AtlantiCare); developer <-> NJBPU for the declaratory ruling confirming non-utility status
mechanisms.term: Not fixed by the ruling; the commercial instrument is a single PPA covering the entire host campus
mechanisms.price_form: $/kWh under a single PPA, plus statutory exemption from the Societal Benefits Charge, Market Transition Charge and Transition Bond Charge

precedents.name: In re Cooper Hospital System — the single-end-user doctrine this ruling extends
precedents.size: CHP plant at One Cooper Plaza serving Three Cooper Plaza, separated by Haddon Avenue; three entities held to constitute one 'end user'
precedents.note: 2017 N.J. PUC LEXIS 74, decided 2017-04-21, cited by both ACE and the Board in QO20030191. The rule extracted from it: all entities in the project must function as part of a single integrated system to be deemed a single end user. ACE argued the Board had warned that going further risked 'a proliferation of mini utilities'; the Board went further anyway.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Admits a reactor on its face, and is the most directly useful commercial mechanism in this file. EDECA's definition opens with 'A generation facility, including, but not limited to, a generation facility that produces Class I or Class II renewable energy' — the renewable clause is illustrative, not a limit, so the statute imposes no fuel, efficiency or emissions test at all. What it does impose is the thing that actually kills reactor deals: 'An on-site generation facility shall not be considered a public utility' holds only for a single end-use customer on contiguous property. A microreactor sized for a campus will overproduce for one host, and the moment a second unrelated offtaker appears the developer becomes a regulated public utility inside someone else's exclusive franchise — the 'proliferation of unregulated mini-utilities' Rate Counsel warned about. The workaround the Board has now blessed twice is corporate, not technical: aggregate the buildings into one end user by common parent and integrated operation (Cooper: three entities, one user; DCO: hospital plus Medical Arts Building, one campus). Note also N.J.S.A. 48:3-77.1: power sold to an off-site end-use thermal customer must ride the incumbent utility's existing distribution infrastructure, so there is no private-wire route out.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: A 6 MW plant serving one hospital campus under one PPA is the exact commercial shape a 1-20 MW reactor is built for, and this ruling shows the whole structure working with a real regulator, a real opponent and a real host. Two microreactor-specific caveats. The contiguity doctrine that rescued DCO — sit across the street and you are still 'on-site' — is worth less to a reactor than to a CHP plant, because a reactor's siting envelope is set by its own exclusion-area and emergency-planning requirements rather than by property lines, and no amount of statutory contiguity relaxes those. And the single-end-user rule bites harder the larger the unit relative to the host: a reactor sized to a campus load has no lawful way to sell its surplus to the building next door unless that building is inside the same corporate family.
blockers: N.J.S.A. 48:3-51 permits exactly ONE end-use customer per on-site generation facility

N.J.S.A. 48:3-77.1 forces sales to an off-site end-use thermal customer onto the incumbent utility's existing distribution infrastructure — no private wire
The incumbent EDC will intervene: ACE argued the petition was procedurally improper, relied on contingent future facts, and prejudged the parallel TCDER II proceeding
